title: Inspector Matadeen on the Moon and Other Satires

access.edition_or_version: Manas Books, 1994; reissued Katha Press, 2003; translated by C. M. Naim

mechanics.premise: Selected comic-satirical stories and sketches in which ordinary, stolid characters are placed in bureaucratic, mystical, or supernatural situations that expose social absurdity.
mechanics.reader_promise: Direct, plain-style Hindi comedy with a sharp critical edge, often built on a deadpan bureaucratic tone.
mechanics.opening: Stories often open with a flat, matter-of-fact situation whose normalcy the narrator maintains even as events become absurd.
mechanics.point_of_view: A plain, unpretentious narrator who reports absurdity without surprise, holding comic distance.
mechanics.character_system: Bureaucrats, clerks, mystics, and ordinary citizens whose literal-mindedness drives the comedy.
mechanics.conflict_and_stakes: Everyday social and institutional pressure, inflated into absurd consequence by the characters' logic.
mechanics.structure: The comic-satirical short story: a single literal premise pursued to an absurd, often grimly funny, conclusion.
mechanics.comic_system: Mundane and bureaucratic imagery against a high or supernatural subject; mock-formal escalation; understatement.
mechanics.dialogue: Plain modern Hindi speech registers; translation limits claims about idiom and wordplay.
mechanics.setting: Twentieth-century Indian civic, rural, and bureaucratic life.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Concrete low-register imagery against elevated subject (D9); mock-formal escalation (D2); understatement.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Normalcy -> literal pursuit -> absurd escalation -> dry, sometimes bleak, punchline.
mechanics.comic_escalation: Heightens one bureaucratic or logical rule to its extreme.
mechanics.climax: The literal logic reaches an absurd extreme.
mechanics.ending: A terse comic-satirical turn that exposes the absurdity.
mechanics.conventions: Central to the modern Hindi vyangya (satirical) tradition; Parsai is described as having revolutionised Hindi satire.
mechanics.innovation_or_subversion: Applies a plain, unadorned style to high absurdity, using bureaucratic register as the vehicle of comedy.
mechanics.critical_reception: Parsai won the Sahitya Akademi Award (1982) for Viklaang Shraddha ka Daur; his work is widely taught and anthologised.
mechanics.audience_reception: Adapted for television and included in Indian school curricula; a continuing popular presence.
mechanics.translation_note: Technique is assessed from C. M. Naim's English renderings; original-language idiom and wordplay are not claimed.
mechanics.boundary_note: Parsai is strongly satirical as well as comic; the record is used for comic mechanism, not as evidence of targetless comedy.
